Listen to this article Share Fura da Nono is one of Northern Nigeria’s most cherished traditional foods and beverages. It is a nutritious, refreshing, culturally significant combination of millet dough balls (fura) and fermented cow’s milk (nono). This nutritious drink is very popular among the Hausa and Fulani communities, and has remained an important part of Northern Nigerian food culture for generations. The traditional drink represents the indigenous food knowledge, pastoral traditions, local agriculture, food processing and community identity of Northern Nigeria From the millet fields and cattle-rearing traditions of Northern Nigeria, Fura da Nono is more than a traditional drink; it is a living expression of Nigeria’s rich culinary heritage and a worthy candidate for consideration under UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage framework. In the bustling markets, neighbourhoods and roadside food stalls of Northern Nigeria, this traditional delicacy continues to hold its place in the country’s culinary landscape. Served chilled or at ambient temperature, depending on local preference and preparation, Fura as it is popularly called, is a distinctive combination of soft, spiced millet dough balls and naturally fermented cow’s milk. Its creamy consistency, slightly sour dairy flavour and characteristic aroma, make it one of the most recognisable traditional food products associated with the Hausa and Fulani communities. Yet, beyond its refreshing taste and nutritional appeal lies a much deeper story of indigenous food science, agricultural adaptation, pastoral culture, women’s entrepreneurship and the intergenerational transmission of culinary knowledge. At a time when countries are increasingly recognising food as an important expression of cultural identity, Fura da Nono deserves greater attention as part of Nigeria’s efforts to document, preserve, promote and internationally showcase its indigenous culinary traditions. The name itself tells the story of its two principal components. Fura refers to the cooked, spiced millet dough formed into small balls, while Nono refers to the fermented milk traditionally obtained from cow’s milk. Together, they produce a cereal-and-dairy delicacy that has remained an important part of food culture in Northern Nigeria. The precise date or individual responsible for the invention of Fura da Nono is not established in available historical records. It is therefore more accurate to understand its origins through the long-standing agricultural and pastoral traditions of the Northern, particularly the relationship between Fulani cattle-rearing communities and the grain-farming populations of the region. For generations, cattle have been central to Fulani pastoral livelihoods, providing milk and other resources that support household nutrition and local economies. In communities where fresh milk was readily available, fermentation became an important indigenous method of processing and preserving milk, extending its usability and creating products with distinctive flavours and textures. At the same time, millet became an important cereal in the semi-arid environments of Northern Nigeria. Its suitability to relatively dry growing conditions made it a significant component of traditional diets. The combination of millet and fermented milk represents a practical relationship between the region’s agricultural resources, food preferences and traditional methods of processing available ingredients. Historical and food-science literature identifies Fura as a traditional staple among Hausa and Fulani communities, with millet, particularly the variety locally known as gero, serving as a principal ingredient. Fura da Nono is not simply an accidental mixture of two ingredients, but a reflection of generations of accumulated knowledge about cereal processing, dairy fermentation, flavour development, food preservation and the use of locally available agricultural products. Although closely associated with Fulani culinary culture, Fura da Nono has also become part of the wider food culture of Northern Nigeria, particularly among Hausa-speaking communities and other populations that have adopted and adapted the delicacy. Its popularity demonstrates how food traditions can travel across communities while retaining important elements of their original cultural identity. The preparation of Fura da Nono is a traditional culinary process involving several stages of food processing. It requires knowledge of grain selection, milling, spice combinations, dough consistency, cooking, pounding and dairy fermentation. The process begins with millet grains, which are carefully selected, cleaned and washed to remove dirt and unwanted materials. Depending on the preferred preparation method, the grains may be dehulled before being dried and milled into flour. The millet flour is then combined with water and traditional spices. Ginger is particularly important, while cloves and dried pepper may also be included, depending on the recipe and the producer’s preference. These ingredients contribute to the characteristic aroma, flavour and warmth of the finished product. Water is gradually incorporated into the spiced flour to form a firm dough. The dough is shaped by hand into balls of varying sizes and cooked in boiling water until properly done. The cooked millet dough is subsequently pounded in a mortar using a pestle, with small quantities of water added as necessary to achieve a smooth, cohesive and slightly elastic consistency. It is then shaped into balls and lightly dusted with millet flour to prevent sticking. The second major component is nono, the traditional fermented cow’s milk. Fresh milk is fermented through the activity of naturally occurring or deliberately introduced microorganisms, depending on the production method. Fermentation produces lactic acid, which gives the milk its characteristic sour taste and changes its texture. In traditional dairy processing, the cream may be separated from the fermented milk. The cream, locally known in Fulani dairy culture as man shanu, is processed into traditional butter, while the remaining fermented milk is consumed as nono. To serve Fura da Nono, the millet balls are broken into smaller pieces or mashed and combined with the fermented milk. The mixture is stirred until the desired consistency is achieved. Some consumers prefer a relatively smooth drink, while others enjoy it with small pieces of millet dough remaining. Sugar may be added to taste, although this is a matter of personal and regional preference. The result is usually a distinctive cereal-and-dairy preparation that combines the earthy taste of millet, the aromatic character of spices and the tangy creaminess of fermented milk. Essentially, the preparation is not entirely uniform. Recipes, spice proportions, textures, fermentation methods and serving preferences may vary between families, producers and communities. Such variations are part of the living nature of culinary traditions. One of the important characteristics of Fura da Nono is its combination of two food groups with complementary nutritional contributions. Millet is a nutrient-containing cereal that provides carbohydrates, dietary fibre, plant protein and minerals. Its carbohydrate content makes it an important source of dietary energy, while its fibre contributes to normal digestive function and helps support a balanced diet. Millet also contains minerals such as magnesium, phosphorus and iron, although the quantities available in a serving depend on the millet variety, processing method and portion size. The grain contains B-group vitamins and various bioactive plant compounds. Its nutritional composition makes it a valuable indigenous cereal, particularly in communities where millet has traditionally served as a staple food. The nono component contributes another important dimension to the nutritional profile. Fermented cow’s milk provides high-quality dairy protein, calcium, phosphorus and other nutrients associated with milk. Protein is essential for the growth, maintenance and repair of body tissues, while calcium and phosphorus contribute to the development and maintenance of healthy bones and teeth. Dairy products can also provide vitamin B12 and riboflavin, although the precise nutritional composition of nono varies with the milk used and the processing conditions. Fermentation is another important aspect of its nutritional and technological value. During fermentation, microorganisms convert some of the lactose in milk into lactic acid. This process produces the characteristic sour taste and influences the texture and microbial composition of the product. Depending on the microorganisms involved and the handling conditions, fermented milk may contain beneficial live cultures. However, not every traditionally fermented product has a standardised probiotic content. The presence of beneficial microorganisms must be established through appropriate scientific testing. The combination of millet and fermented milk therefore provides carbohydrates, protein, fibre and minerals within one traditional food preparation. Its nutritional contribution, however, depends on the proportions of fura and nono, the quantity consumed and whether additional sugar is introduced. Fura da Nono can form part of a varied and balanced diet, but it should not be presented as a cure for any disease or as a substitute for medical treatment. Its nutritional value is particularly relevant to discussions about food security, local food systems and the promotion of indigenous crops. Millet is an important climate-adapted cereal in many dryland agricultural systems, while traditional dairy processing provides opportunities to add value to locally produced milk. By bringing these ingredients together, Fura da Nono illustrates how traditional food knowledge can contribute to dietary diversity and the utilisation of indigenous agricultural resources. An essential part of the Fura da Nono story is the contribution of women who have sustained its production, processing and distribution across generations. In many Fulani communities, women have traditionally played significant roles in milk processing and dairy trade. Knowledge of milking, fermentation, cream separation, butter production and the preparation of nono is often transmitted within families, particularly from mothers and older female relatives to younger generations. Women are also central to the preparation and sale of Fura da Nono in markets, neighbourhoods and other commercial spaces. Through small-scale businesses, they have helped maintain the availability of the delicacy while generating income for their households. Their contribution extends beyond selling a traditional drink. They are custodians of specialised knowledge, including the selection of ingredients, control of fermentation, determination of product consistency, use of traditional utensils and understanding of consumer preferences. This knowledge is not always written down or formally taught in institutions. It is frequently acquired through observation, participation and repeated practice. Such informal systems of learning are precisely the kinds of cultural transmission that make traditional food practices valuable subjects for intangible cultural heritage documentation. The women who prepare and sell Fura da Nono should therefore be recognised not merely as food vendors but as practitioners and knowledge bearers whose experiences, techniques and oral histories deserve documentation and preservation. Fura da Nono occupies an important place within this diversity because it represents the intersection of cereal agriculture and pastoral dairy culture. Its preparation preserves knowledge about millet cultivation, grain processing, traditional spices, milk fermentation and food presentation. Its consumption reflects established dietary preferences, while its commercial distribution supports small-scale food enterprises. The tradition also offers an opportunity to tell a more comprehensive story about Northern Nigerian food culture beyond the familiar narratives of popular dishes. For international audiences, Fura da Nono can provide insight into the communities that developed practical methods of combining locally available ingredients into nutritious and culturally meaningful foods. It is also an opportunity to promote Nigerian food journalism, food tourism, travel journalism encourage investment in local millet and dairy value chains, and create wider markets for indigenous food product However, its heritage value should not be measured only by its commercial potential. Let’s visit the kitchen Recipe for 6 servings: – 6 Cups Millet grains or millet flour – 8 Fresh gingers – 10 Cloves – 1 teaspoon dried pepper (optional) – Water – A little millet flour for dusting For the Nono – 6 Cups Fresh cow’s milk, preferably safely pasteurised milk for household preparation – A suitable starter culture or previously prepared nono from a hygienically controlled source Method Step 1: Preparing the millet The millet grains are carefully sorted to remove stones, dirt and other unwanted materials. They are washed and, where necessary, dehulled before being dried and milled into flour. Step 2: Adding traditional spices The millet flour is combined with ground ginger, cloves and, depending on individual preference, a little dried pepper. These spices give fura its characteristic aroma and distinctive taste. The proportions vary according to family recipes and regional preferences. Step 3: Making the dough Water is gradually added to the spiced millet flour until a firm; workable dough is formed. The dough is divided into portions and shaped into balls. Step 4: Cooking the millet balls The shaped dough balls are placed in boiling water and cooked until thoroughly done. They are then removed and allowed to cool sufficiently for handling. Step 5: Pounding and shaping The cooked millet dough is transferred into a traditional mortar and pounded with a pestle. Small quantities of water may be introduced during pounding to produce a smooth, cohesive and slightly elastic consistency. The resulting dough is divided into smaller balls and lightly dusted with millet flour to prevent sticking. These are the traditional fura balls. Step 6: Preparing the fermented milk The second component, nono, is produced through the fermentation of cow’s milk. Traditionally, fermentation relies on established indigenous practices and naturally occurring or previously introduced lactic acid bacteria. The milk is allowed to ferment under controlled hygienic conditions until it develops its characteristic mildly sour taste and texture. Where traditional fermentation is practised, the preparation should be protected from contamination, with appropriate attention to temperature, cleanliness and safe handling. In traditional Fulani dairy processing, the cream may be separated from the fermented milk. This cream, known as man shanu, is processed into traditional butter, while the remaining fermented milk is consumed as nono. Step 7: Combining the Fura and Nono To prepare the drink, the fura balls are broken into smaller pieces and placed in a clean bowl or serving container. The fermented milk is poured over them. The mixture is stirred and gently mashed until the desired consistency is achieved. Some consumers prefer a smooth, creamy drink, while others prefer to retain small pieces of millet dough. Sugar may be added according to individual taste, although it is not essential to the traditional preparation. Step 8: Serving Fura da Nono can be served chilled or at ambient temperature, depending on local preference. It is traditionally enjoyed as a refreshing meal accompaniment, a filling snack or a nourishing drink. The preparation is not completely standardised. The proportions of millet, spices and fermented milk, as well as the texture and serving style, vary among households and producers. These differences are important expressions of the living nature of the tradition.
